title: Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 28 Aug 2026]
    Title:Automated Researchers Can Reliably Mitigate Alignment Failures
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Automating alignment research may accelerate progress toward aligned AI, but whether it does is hard to measure. Luckily, many alignment failures, such as deception, sycophancy, and jailbreaks, are already measurable by public benchmarks. We study whether automated alignment researchers (AARs) can post-train to mitigate alignment failures by proposing training methods and data to simultaneously optimize multiple safety benchmarks, while preserving general capability. Across 10 alignment failures, the strongest AAR methods significantly reduce the targeted alignment failures and generalize to a held-out benchmark, multi-turn behavioral audits, and models up to 4.7 times larger than the target model. As a human baseline, 28 experienced researchers receive up to eight hours to develop methods for the same benchmarks, but their methods underperform the best AAR methods. Using human ideas as the AARs' initial research direction does not improve performance, suggesting current AARs may not need guidance from experienced researchers. These results suggest that automating alignment research on well-characterized failures may be practical in the near term.

report.summary: Automated AI researchers outperform human experts at mitigating alignment failures, showing automated alignment research is practical for well-characterized benchmarks.
report.background: As AI systems grow more capable, aligning them with human intent becomes harder. Alignment failures—deception, sycophancy, jailbreaks—are increasingly measurable via public benchmarks, but fixing them usually requires labor-intensive human research. This paper tests whether automated alignment researchers (AARs), AI systems that propose training methods and data, can post-train models to reduce these failures without degrading general ability. The researchers compared AARs against 28 experienced human researchers given up to eight hours. AARs not only matched but outperformed humans across ten alignment failures, generalized to held-out benchmarks and larger models, and gained no benefit from human-provided research seeds. This suggests a near-term path where AI systems help solve their own alignment, shifting the research bottleneck from human effort to benchmark design and validation.
key_points: Across ten alignment failure benchmarks, the strongest automated alignment researchers (AARs) significantly reduced targeted failures while preserving general capability. This implies the AARs found training methods and data that are effective for multiple safety issues simultaneously, rather than overfitting to one benchmark.

AAR methods generalized to a held-out benchmark, multi-turn behavioral audits, and models up to 4.7 times larger than the target model. This is a key sign the fixes are not superficial—they address underlying behavior rather than memorized benchmark patterns.

AARs outperformed 28 experienced human researchers who had up to eight hours to develop methods for the same benchmarks. The human baseline underperformed the best AAR methods, suggesting that in well-characterized, benchmark-driven alignment tasks, automation can exceed expert human effort in both scale and reliability.

Using human ideas as the AARs' initial research direction did not improve performance, suggesting current AARs may not need guidance from experienced researchers. This reduces the barrier to scaling automated alignment research and hints that AI-generated research directions are already sufficiently diverse and effective.

The authors conclude that automating alignment research on well-characterized failures may be practical in the near term. This is a shift from viewing alignment as a purely human-driven endeavor to one where AI systems are active participants in their own safety improvements.

An important caveat is that the benchmarks measure known, well-defined failures. The paper does not claim AARs can solve unknown or emergent alignment risks, which remain harder to specify and validate.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this suggests that safety teams can deploy automated systems to continuously scan for known failure modes and automatically propose and test mitigations, greatly accelerating the loop between discovering a vulnerability and patching it. Developers would gain tools that reduce the need for large human research teams for benchmark-defined safety tasks, lowering alignment costs and making safety improvements more accessible to smaller labs. For regular users, this could mean faster and more robust fixes for chatbots behaving deceptively or being jailbroken, with measurable improvements in trustworthiness. However, it also raises a cautionary point: if automation works well for measurable failures, the field must invest heavily in building comprehensive, high-quality benchmarks and audits, since these automated researchers will only be as good as the targets they are optimized against. Blind spots in benchmarks could become hidden gaps in safety.
report.tools: Readers can explore public alignment benchmarks used in this line of work, such as the HarmBench and BBH for jailbreaks and behavioral safety, via their GitHub repositories. For building automated researchers, frameworks like OpenAI's o1 or Anthropic's Claude with tool use can prototype AAR loops. Try the Python library 'evals' (OpenAI) for running model evaluations, or use Hugging Face's leaderboard libraries to track safety benchmark performance and reproduce multi-objective post-training experiments.
